messages.text: Catalogue the new arrivals
Pell has a crate of unsorted pamphlets and the expression of a man who has been looking at it for a week.
You are too tired for that. Sleep, eat, or sit down for a while.
Sort the crate
A box of pamphlets turns out to be entirely love poetry, anonymous and bad. You file it under Natural History and Pell does not correct you.
By the end of the afternoon you can tell a forgery from a copy by smell. Pell lets you ink the date on the new index himself.
You sort by date, then by hand, then by what you suspect the author was ashamed of. Pell is quietly delighted, and pays you in coins and silence.
A riddle from the shelves

{#select n}{#case 1}Pell slides a card across the desk. It reads: "I have cities, but no houses; mountains, but no trees; water, but no fish."{#case 2}The second card reads: "The more you take, the more you leave behind."{#case 3}The third card reads, in a smaller hand: "What can be broken without being held, and kept only when given?"{#default}A card.{/select}
The words slide around in your head without settling.
Answer it
Make a guess
"A map," you say. Pell's eyebrows go up a fraction. "The last person to solve that one took a week."
"Footsteps." Pell breathes out through his nose, which is applause. He gives you four coins from a drawer that is not a till.
"A promise." Pell takes off his spectacles to look at you, and you realise that for the first time he is looking at a person.
"A... country?" Pell sets the card aside with a small, kind, devastating cough.
"Fear?" you try. Pell considers this with enormous courtesy. "Not unreasonable. Not correct."
"A... window?" Pell closes his eyes for a moment, as though in prayer, and passes you a biscuit.
The locked shelf
Behind Pell's desk is a glass-fronted cabinet. He has never opened it in front of anyone. Today he has left the key on the blotter and his back turned.
The old script swims. You can tell it is important and not why.
Read what is inside
Pell has been persuaded by better, and by worse. You have not got it in you yet.
Ask Pell to open it for you
A survey of the old quarry, with a bridge pier marked in red and a cache drawn as a small neat X. A page is torn from the ledger beside it; you note the shape of the tear.
You make your case, which is mostly that you would like very much to see a map. Pell regards you for the length of a long breath. "Copy it," he says. "Do not make me regret it."
Ask Pell about the banner
Pell keeps the town's accounts. Nobody has ever asked him whether they are all in order.
Ask about the festival ledger
A page is missing from the festival ledger. The supplies line. Someone needed to know where the banner was stored, and then someone needed to forget I had written it down.
The tear is clean. Tailor's scissors, I would say, or a dyer's.
Where do you come from?
Aunt Odile pours the tea and waits. "Tell me about home," she says. "Properly, now. Who raised you?"
Farming folk: long days, strong backs
Merchants: a ledger in every pocket
Scholars: more books than furniture
Dock folk: salt, rope and stubbornness
Gentry fallen on hard times: manners, no money
What were you like as a child?
Odile studies you over the rim of her cup. "And what were you like? Not what you were told. What you were."
The bookish one: always reading, always asking why
The athletic one: always climbing something
The charmer: always talking your way out
The scrappy loner: you managed fine alone
What is your first quirk?
“Everyone has a habit,” says Odile. “What is yours?”
And a second quirk?
“And another,” says Odile. “One is a habit. Two is a personality.”
Spare effort
You have {#plural left}{#one}one point{#other}{left} points{/plural} of spare effort to spend before the summer starts.
You have no points left to spend.
+5 Strength
You have no points left to spend.
+5 Wits
You have no points left to spend.
+5 Charm
You have no points left to spend.
+5 Grit
Spend all of your points first.
That is everything
How do you dress?
Odile finds you a mirror. "Well? What will they see when you walk into the square?"
Plain and comfortable
Practical: sleeves rolled, boots laced
Neat: collar, waistcoat, a pen in the pocket
Ready?
“There you are,” says Odile. “That is who is going to the Trials.”
Begin the summer
Start over
Unload the herring boat
The boat-master is a woman with arms like rope and a voice like a gate. "Crates," she says. "Fast."
You are too tired for that. Sleep, eat, or sit down for a while.
Carry crates
The second boat is mostly eels. You learn that you can carry a crate of them on your shoulder if you do not think about the lid.
The boat-master tosses you a crate without asking. By the afternoon you are the one who is calling "Fast" to the newer hands.
Sixty crates, two buckets of ice and a long afternoon. You are paid in coins and a smell you will carry for a week.
Fish off the end of the pier
A rod leans against a bollard where somebody forgot it. The river is the colour of tea.
Sit and wait
A heron stands twenty feet away and fishes better than you. You exchange a look, and it is entirely professional.
You catch a trout so large that you hold it up to be sure. Nobody is looking. You let it go, and feel better than if they had.
You catch nothing for two hours, then something small and furious. The patience gets into your bones, and with it a kind of calm that has not been there in days.
The broken bridge
The old bridge to the quarry has a gap in the middle the width of a cart. A crowd of sensible people has gathered to agree that something should be done.
You can see what the bridge needs, or you can lift it, but not both yet.
Plan and haul a new span
They are listening, politely. But they are not yet listening to you.
Rally the town to mend it
Carpenters cost fifteen coins and do not take promises.
Hire the carpenters
A day of drawing in the dust, then of timber and rope and a great deal of swearing. When the last plank is pegged, the whole dockside walks across it, one by one, in a kind of ceremony.
You stand on a crate and say what everyone is thinking. By evening there are forty people and a cart of planks. The bridge is mended before the sun goes down and you have somehow become its mother.
The carpenters take your coins and do it in a morning. It is a perfectly good bridge. It is not a story anyone will tell.
The ferryman
The ferryman smokes a clay pipe and watches everyone come and go. He has seen more of Hollowbrook than the constable.
He nods at you, says nothing, and goes back to his pipe.
Ask about the early boat
Lad with a long bundle took the first crossing to the quarry road. Said he was delivering linen. Linen does not clink like brass poles.
The ferryman shrugs when you thank him, as if he had said nothing at all.
The Trials end with every guild holding out a hand, and a whole town unsure which to look at.
A bridge mended, a banner returned, three Trials passed. The town has a name for people like that, and it is not a name I am allowed to say in the square.
Hollowbrook remembers, my dear. I told you so.
You stay in Hollowbrook that autumn, and then the next. Over the years your name goes on a bench and a bridge and a rather good cheese.
I do not take apprentices. I have taken you. Do not make me explain it to the guild.
The forge becomes your world: iron and ash, a fire that never goes out, and a woman who nods at things she approves of. By the second winter, she nods at you.
I am old. The shelves are many. The ledger has been waiting for a hand like yours, and I have been waiting for someone who would see why it matters.
You become the second keeper of the Hollowbrook archive, a post no one has noticed is a kind of power until it is yours.
The guild of players wants you for the autumn circuit. Eleven towns, no beds, terrible food. Say yes.
You say yes. You say yes in a doorway, with a fiddle in your hand and a crowd already shouting for the song about the goose.
The town watch is short of people who can run and think and say no to a neighbour. I would like you on it. Do not say it is a bad offer.
You take the badge. The first night on duty, an old woman gives you soup. The second, you find the thing that has been going wrong in the lamp-oil supply. By the third, you belong here.
Well. That was a summer. Did you learn anything?

You did, as it turns out. A little about lifting and a little about lying and quite a lot about asking for help. You leave in the autumn with a better pair of boots and an invitation to come back next year.
Thirty coins. It was thirty coins, my dear. Next year, then.
You watch the Trials from the back, and you watch someone else lift the wheel, and someone else give the Address. It is a very good festival. It would have been a better one from the stage.
Work Mara's bellows
Mara jerks her chin at the great leather lungs of the forge. "Pump," she says. "Even. Not like a goose."
You are too tired for that. Sleep, eat, or sit down for a while.
Pump until she tells you to stop
Your arms burn by the tenth minute and weep by the thirtieth. Mara says "Even," four times, and by the end it is almost true.
Mara stops you with two fingers on the lever. "Listen," she says. The fire is breathing with you now. For a second it is not work at all.
You find the rhythm and the fire answers it, a long white breath. Mara nods at the flames, which is how she nods at you.
The anvil
In the corner stands a small anvil with a rope handle on its horn. Apprentices are measured by it. Mara does not mention it, which is how you know it matters.
The anvil does not so much as rock. It would take someone stronger.
Lift it to your chest
Heave anyway
It comes up grudgingly, then all at once, and you stand in the forge with a hundredweight of iron against your chest and your heart going like a hammer.
Mara looks at the anvil, then at you, then at the anvil. "Put it down gently," she says. "It has been through enough."
The anvil moves a hand's breadth and thinks better of it. You sit down very suddenly. Somewhere, a smith is not laughing.
Mara offers to teach you
messages.when: at(:player, :forge), free_time(), flag(:anvil_lifted), quality(:mara, :trust, ?t), ?t >= 2, not technique(:leverage)

messages.text: Mara wipes her hands on her apron. "You lift like someone who is going to hurt herself," she says. "Stand there."
messages.when: at(:player, :forge), free_time(), flag(:anvil_lifted), quality(:mara, :trust, ?t), ?t >= 2, not technique(:leverage)

messages.text: Learn the trick of leverage
Strength is a fraction of the work. A bar, a block and a good place to stand: that is the rest.
Again. Feet under you. Good. Now you are only half as stupid as you were an hour ago.
A cracked lock
A strongbox sits open on the bench, its lock a puzzle of broken wards. "Customer's," says Mara. "I do iron, not fiddly."
You turn the wards over and cannot tell which are meant to be broken.
Mend the lock
Do your best
The trick is to listen to the lock rather than to your hands. Three small clicks, and the box opens as if embarrassed.
Mara pays you eight coins and says only, "Not bad." You take it for a speech.
Something snaps. It was either the right ward or the wrong one. Mara looks at the lock for a long time and then at you.
Ask Mara about the banner
Mara's forge has a view of half the square, and she has never in her life looked at anything she did not mean to.
Ask what she saw
Somebody carried a bundle out of the square before dawn. Rough sacking. Hands stained purple to the wrist, the kind of purple dyers cannot get off in a week.
I did not stop him. I assumed it was laundry. Tell Hask I said so, and tell him I am sorry.
Help Aunt Odile with the chores
A list in Odile's slanting hand is pinned to the door: wood, water, the east fence, the hens.{#if query trait(:family, :farm)} You could do all of it in your sleep.{/if}
You are too tired for that. Sleep, eat, or sit down for a while.
Work through the list
The hens are in revolt. You negotiate, cluck back, and are paid in eggs and a long lecture on the east fence, which you did not touch.
Odile watches you carry the water without being asked. "You have your mother's habit of not complaining," she says, and hands you a second slice of bread.
Wood split, water hauled, the east fence propped with a plank you will have to apologise to later. Odile inspects it all and gives you three coins and a look you decide to treat as pride.
Read your father's books
A shelf over the bed holds the books he left you. The spines are cracked in the places he loved.
You are too tired for that. Sleep, eat, or sit down for a while.
Read until the candle gutters
You read about tides and tithes and the correct use of a comma. Some of it even stays. Most of what stays is the comma.
A treatise on weights and measures turns out to be a love letter to precision. You begin to notice how often the market's scales are lying.
You find your father's own margin notes, argued in pencil with a dead author. By the third page you have joined the argument, and you are winning.
Cook dinner for the house
Odile is dozing in her chair. The pantry has onions, a heel of cheese and an ambition.
Make something worth eating
You try a soup. It is, at first, a rumour of a soup. By the second taste it has become something that belongs to the table.
Odile eats in silence, and then asks for the recipe. You tell her you have none, and she says that is exactly what she was afraid of.
The onions are a triumph. The cheese is a compromise. Odile eats two helpings and says nothing, which from her is a song.
Odile has something to tell you
Odile puts down her knitting and looks at you for a long moment. "There is something of your father's that I kept," she says.
Sit with her and listen
He left Hollowbrook the summer of his own Trials. He did not win, and he never said why. He sent these back, wrapped in a note I never answered.
Spectacles. Nothing grand. But he wrote that clear sight was the whole of cleverness. I think he meant you.
{place}
You are not tired; there is nothing to recover.
Take a breath on a bench
Go to {to}
Go
The way to {to} is closed
{#select to}{#case quarry}The bridge is out. It will have to be mended before anyone crosses it.{#case green}The Green is roped off until the eve of the festival.{#default}The way is closed.{/select}
Try it anyway
Go to bed
Sleep until morning
The bell rings: the Trials begin
The bell on the Festival Green rings three times. Everyone in Hollowbrook turns the same way at once.
Walk to the Green
Day two. Odile has left a note on the table: bread in the cloth, trouble in the square, do not be late for either.
Day three. A cart of apples tipped over in the lane before dawn. The whole street smells like cider and apology.
Day four. Your muscles remember yesterday in detail. The cat sits on your chest and pronounces judgment.
Day five. Halfway. Posters for the Trials have multiplied overnight, each one slightly crueller than the last.
Day six. A grey morning, and a rumour already on every doorstep. Nobody will say what it is.
Day seven. Rain on the roof, soft as a drum brush. The river has risen and the docks smell of old wood.
Day eight. The whole town has started rehearsing in public. A man is reciting a speech to a goat.
Day nine. The last full day. Someone has hung lanterns along the road to the Green, and for the first time the Trials feel less like a threat than a promise.
Midsummer. The sun comes up like it has been rehearsing too. By evening the whole of Hollowbrook will be on the Green, and so will you.
The fishmonger's scales
The fishmonger's thumb has been on the scale for thirty years. He sees you notice, and does not lift it.
The fishmonger has heard better patter from his own parrot.
Out-talk him
Try to haggle
You talk about the weather, his daughter, the price of salt and the injustice of a thumb. By the end he is paying you to stop, and you have fourteen coins and an enemy for life.
He gives you three coins and a fish you did not ask for, and you leave unsure whether that was winning.
Mind a stall
A cheese seller needs her stall minded while she "checks on a cousin". The cousin is apparently the tavern.
You are too tired for that. Sleep, eat, or sit down for a while.
Mind the stall
A man buys a cheese for the sole purpose of telling you it was not very good. You thank him for his custom and he is moved to buy another.
By noon you have regulars. By two, a small queue. The seller returns to find you with the till, a joke and nobody worried.
You sell eleven wedges, one wheel and an opinion of the cheese that is entirely yours. The seller returns pink and cheerful and pays you six coins.
A hand in a pocket
A quick shape slides through the crowd, and the weight of your purse changes in a way you notice a second too late.
You do not have the legs, or the nerve, for a chase through that crowd.
Run the thief down
You open your mouth. The market is much too loud.
Shout for the constable
Let it go

Three stalls, a barrow, a flight of steps and a very surprised goose. You catch the thief by the collar at the fountain, and take back more than he took. Constable Hask arrives to find the matter entirely concluded.
"STOP, THIEF!" turns the whole market into a net. The thief is caught by a cheese seller with a shovel. Hask takes your name down, with approval.
You decide that whatever he took is the price of not running. Your purse is lighter and your feet are unhurt, and you learn a thing about the market that is worth more than the coins.
A crying child by the well
A small child in a stolen hat is sitting by the well, being very brave in the loudest way possible.
Find her family

Her cousin is Tilly Marsh, who runs the tavern, and who hugs the child so hard the hat flies off. Tilly looks at you for a moment longer than she needs to. "I owe you," she says. In Hollowbrook that is a currency.
For sale: {item}
The stallholder holds it up so the light catches it. "{cost} coins," she says, "and you will not find better."
You cannot afford it, or your pockets are full (three things at most).
Buy it
The coins change hands and so does a little of your attention. You tuck it away and the stallholder is already looking at someone else.
The north wall
A rusted ring is set in the north wall, forty feet up, where the stone is as smooth as a table. The map had an X exactly there.
You get ten feet up and know, with the perfect clarity of a falling person, that you will not get further.
Climb for the ring
Try it anyway

Hand over hand, with your fingertips as the only argument. At the top the ring comes away with a pull, and behind it is a hollow with a leather purse and twenty-five coins of a currency that has since changed its face.
You slide from ten feet, and land in a heap of shale and indignity. The wall is unharmed.
Dane's challenge
Dane Whitlock is stretching on the lip of the quarry like a man who has done this before in front of mirrors. "Rim to the old crane and back," he says. "Loser carries the other's pack."
You do not have the lungs for the loop, and he does.
Take the bet
Run it anyway
You run the way you did as a child: without thinking of the end. At the crane you are a stride ahead. At the rim you are two.
Huh. You can really run. I had you down as the book-and-ribbon sort. Don't tell anyone I said that.
Dane is a crack of speed at the first bend and a spot on the horizon by the second. You arrive to find him sitting on your pack.
Good effort. Truly. Carry mine, would you?
The stars from the quarry floor
The walls shut out the town. Above you, the sky is a ceiling full of the same few stories.
Lie back and watch
A meteor draws a line of white across the bowl of the sky, and is gone before you can wish for anything useful.
You fall asleep, and wake with frost on your sleeve and the whole sky turned a quarter-circle. You had forgotten you had not been anywhere.
The quarry holds the dark like a bowl. You count satellites that are not there yet and the names of things you have never been told. You leave a little lighter.
Run the quarry steps
There are two hundred and eleven steps cut into the east wall, and nobody has ever thanked them.
You are too tired for that. Sleep, eat, or sit down for a while.
Run them all
Rain makes the steps a different animal. You take them a little more slowly, and a little more carefully, and come down in a better mood than you went up.
You run them with your eyes shut for the last fifty. Your feet know every one by now.
On the second hundred, your thoughts run out. On the two hundred and eleventh you stand over the whole town and feel exactly as tall as you need to be.
Notice: {job}

A strip of paper pinned to the board, in a neat hand: {#select job}{#case carry_barrels}barrels to the cooper's, hands wanted.{#case copy_ledgers}ledgers to be copied fair, steady hand required.{#case greet_visitors}visitors to be greeted and shown to their rooms, pleasant manner required.{#case mind_the_ferry}ferry to be minded while the ferryman sleeps off a wedding.{#default}work.{/select}
You are too tired to take on work today.
Take the job
Forty barrels, one hill and a cooper who counts every one twice. By the end your hands know the shape of oak.
You copy three ledgers and find two errors in the original, one of them theft. You decide it is not your business and then spend an hour worrying.
You greet nineteen visitors by name, and by the third you have begun to mean it. The innkeeper tips you and tells you that you have a gift.
You pole the ferry across forty times and talk to nobody. The river tells you a great deal, but it is not interested in your answers.
The gossip circle
Five people on a bench have the air of a jury that never quite delivers a verdict.
Join the circle
The bench is arguing about whether the baker's bread is better since he stopped talking to his brother. You contribute a position, and are surprised to find you hold it.
They make room for you without being asked. Somebody passes you a bun. For the first time you hear the gossip not as news but as the sound the town makes to know it is alive.
You learn a great deal about a woman's marriage and one useful thing about a man's debts. By the end, you are being invited to a funeral, and you are going.
The constable has heard
Constable Hask is waiting under the lamp-post with the air of a man about to say something he has rehearsed.
Meet his eye
Word gets round, as you will learn. Everyone I trust has told me something good about you before noon.
This is five coins from the town purse. It is not a payment. It is a thank-you in a form I am allowed to give.
A crowd around the festival pole
A knot of people stands around the empty pole where the festival banner should hang. Nobody is talking above a murmur.
Push to the front
It was here at midnight and not at dawn. The banner has hung on that pole for two hundred years and nobody has ever taken it. Until now.
I am short of men and short of time. If you have eyes or a good word, use them, and tell me. Three things, mind. I will not accuse on a hunch.
Tell the constable who took it
messages.when: at(:player, :square), flag(:banner_stolen), not flag(:banner_solved), not flag(:accused_wrong)

messages.text: Hask has set up a desk by the pole and a ledger for names. "Say it plain," he says, "and be sure."
messages.when: at(:player, :square), flag(:banner_stolen), not flag(:banner_solved), not flag(:accused_wrong)

messages.text: You have suspicions, not evidence. Hask wants three things he can write down.
Accuse {who}
A dyer's apprentice, a Whitlock cousin, and a grudge about a disqualification three Trials ago. Of course. It is always something that small.
The banner is recovered, folded in the cousin's own sock drawer. The town owes you a drink. I owe you a better opinion.
I will make enquiries. I will make them quietly, because you have just told me something that was not true in front of a whole square.
People find somewhere else to look.
The Trials entry table
A trestle table by the town hall steps, a clerk with a quill, and a sign: ENTRY FEE THIRTY COINS. NO CREDIT. NO EXCEPTIONS. NO, NOT EVEN YOU.
The fee is thirty coins, and you do not have thirty coins.
Pay the thirty coins
The clerk counts the coins twice, writes your name in a ledger and gives you a wooden token on a string. It weighs almost nothing, and you will feel it all summer.
Open mic at the Heron
A stool, a stub of candle and a crowd that has already forgiven you in advance. Tilly waves you up.
You get to the stool and a cough comes out. Tilly winces for you.
Take the stage
Try a verse
You tell a story about a goose and a bishop. By the end, grown men are wiping their eyes, and the fiddler has started playing under you without being asked.
You forget the second verse, then the first. A kind drunk finishes it for you and everyone claps. It is the nicest humiliation of your life.
The arm-wrestling table
A dockhand the size of a doorframe is taking on all comers, loudly, for a copper a go.
Dockhands do not lose to people who have not been lifting things.
Take the table
Have a go anyway
It is a long ten seconds. Your whole arm turns to light, and then his knuckles touch the wood and the room erupts. He buys you a drink and calls you "boss" for the rest of the night.
He pins you in a heartbeat, and apologises in the way large men do: by buying you something and not looking at your face.
Listen to the tables
The Gilded Heron is a pot of low conversations, and you have a seat by the stove.
Pretend to read a menu
Two sisters argue in whispers about a will. A brewer swears he saw the festival banner on a ladder at midnight. A boy is explaining the Trials to a younger boy and getting it magnificently wrong.
The room is quieter tonight. You hear the clink of a spoon, the fiddle tuning, a single laugh, and in the pauses the whole of a town breathing.
A carter complains about bridge tolls. A tailor's wife complains about her husband's apprentices. A girl in the corner is learning the fiddle from a book. You leave with a head full of a town.
Ask Tilly about the night before
Tilly keeps the one window in the square that stays lit all night.
Ask what she saw from the window
A lad came out of the square at three, carrying something long. Young. Quick. A cousin of someone, I would swear: he had the Whitlock walk.
I did not know it mattered. Tell the constable. And if it is who I think it is, tell him I am sorry too.
The Lifting
A cart wheel taller than you, an axle, and a rope. The judge calls it "the Lifting": raise the wheel to the pegs. Mara is watching, arms folded.
The wheel does not feel your effort. It would take a stronger back.
Lift it with your back
You have not been shown how to make a lever do the lifting.
Use Mara's leverage
You do not have the stubbornness to hold it for that long.
Grind it up
Try your best
The wheel comes up in one long pull and you set it on the pegs without a sound. The crowd's roar is the best weather you have ever stood in.
A block, a bar, a place to stand. The wheel lifts as if it had been waiting to. Mara's mouth does something unfamiliar at one corner.
It takes you a minute and a half and you do not breathe for most of it. The crowd counts with you. When the wheel clicks into the pegs, you do not move for a while.
The wheel moves a hand and sags back. The crowd is kind about it. Somewhere, Mara is looking at her own boots.
The Reckoning
A table with three locked boxes, a ledger and a single sentence on a card: "One of these lies. Which, and how can you tell?" The judge turns the hourglass.
The sentences twist when you try to hold them.
Work it out
You haven't got enough threads to pull on yet.
Reason from what you've learned this week
The judge is not a person who is susceptible to flattery.
Charm the judge into a hint
Guess

Two of the boxes cannot both be telling the truth. The third has a grammatical tell, a small one, that only you and the dead man who wrote it would notice. You say which, and why, and the judge writes it down.
You have spent a week learning how this town lies. It turns out that this is exactly the skill. Three questions, one answer, and the judge puts down her pen.
You do not know the answer, but you know that the judge wants you to. You say a sentence that sounds like the answer and watch her face to learn if it was, and adjust. She is almost grateful.
You choose. You are wrong. You look at the sand in the glass and wonder how it was ever so slow.
The Address
A raised stage, a lantern, and a thousand faces. The judge announces: "The Address. Say something worth the town's attention." The crowd settles like a flock.
You do not yet have the voice to carry across the whole Green.
Speak from the heart
You have never sung in front of anyone in Hollowbrook, and they will notice.
Sing the song from the Heron
Not enough people in town would stand up and say a word for you.
Let your friends speak for you
Say a few words
You talk about arriving, and not knowing a soul, and being fed. You do not remember the end of it. The Green does.
The first note wobbles and then the fiddler from the Heron finds you in the dark, and a thousand people sing the goose-and-bishop chorus back at you.
Tilly stands first. Then Mara, with her arms folded. Then Hask, who has not done this in his life. By the end half the Green has stood up and you have not said anything at all.
You say "thank you" and "I am glad to be here" and then a thing about weather. Polite applause, like rain on a tent.
The judges confer
The judges put their heads together under the lanterns. When they look up, the whole Green holds its breath. "The guilds," says the oldest of them, "offer you the following."
Accept: {e}
You cannot enter
You did not pay the fee, and the clerk has already put away the ledger. You are not one of the people in the square.
Watch from the crowd
Lanterns on every pole, trestle tables and a stage of planks. Hollowbrook has put on its second-best clothes. A drum starts somewhere to your left and you feel it in your teeth.
Order. Order. Three Trials: the Lifting, the Reckoning, the Address. Do them in any order you like. The town will be watching.
Try not to fall over. Or do. I would find it very instructive.
You have a perfectly good view from the back of the Green, and nobody to blame for it.

The cart driver lets you down at the edge of Hollowbrook and does not wait for thanks. Ten days until Midsummer. Ten days until the Trials.
A letter in your pocket says there is a bed for you at your aunt's house, and that the town is short of hands. It does not say what the Trials are for. Everyone you meet will assume you know.
The gatekeeper squints at you. "Name?"
{visitor}! Look at the size of you. Come in, come in. The kettle has been on since breakfast.

You will want to know about the Trials. Three contests on Midsummer night: strength, wits and charm. The guilds sponsor whoever impresses them. Enter, and you will need the fee, and you will need to be good.
That is the spirit. Your mother said the same at your age. Sit; eat; then we will look at what kind of person you have grown into.
The catch is that everyone wants it. Be kind to the people who help you. Hollowbrook remembers.
Sit. Of course sit. There will be time to be tested. Tonight, be a person.
Before the summer begins, you take a moment to decide who you are.
Breakfast is on the table, and the town is waking up. Go and see what it needs of you.
